paragraphs.heading: The science of light
paragraphs.text: Optics is the part of physics that looks at electromagnetic radiation: how it behaves, how it can be controlled, and how it can be detected. That includes how it acts on matter and the instruments that use or sense it. Most of the time optics deals with visible, ultraviolet and infrared light, but it reaches out to radio waves, microwaves and X-rays too. The same word is also used for technology that steers beams of elementary charged particles.

paragraphs.heading: Rays and waves
paragraphs.text: The classical electromagnetic account of light explains most optical effects, but it is often hard to use in practice, so working optics relies on simpler models. The most common, geometric optics, treats light as rays that travel straight and change direction at surfaces, either passing through them or reflecting from them. Physical optics is a fuller model that adds wave effects, such as diffraction and interference, which rays cannot explain. Historically the ray model came first and the wave model followed. In the 19th century, advances in electromagnetic theory showed that light waves are in fact electromagnetic radiation.

paragraphs.heading: Light as particles
paragraphs.text: Some effects only make sense if light behaves both like a wave and like a stream of particles. Explaining them takes quantum mechanics. When light is treated as particles, those particles are called photons. Quantum optics is the field that applies quantum mechanics to optical systems.

paragraphs.heading: Where optics turns up
paragraphs.text: Optics matters in astronomy, many kinds of engineering, photography and medicine, including radiation therapy and CT scans, as well as in eye care fields such as ophthalmology and optometry. In daily life it is built into mirrors, lenses, telescopes, microscopes, lasers and fibre optics.

paragraphs.heading: The first lenses
paragraphs.text: Optics started with lenses made by the ancient Egyptians and Mesopotamians. The oldest known lenses, of polished crystal and often of quartz, come from Crete and date back as far as 2000 BC. Lenses from Rhodes, and Assyrian ones such as the Nimrud lens, date from around 700 BC. The Greeks and Romans made lenses by filling glass spheres with water. The word optics itself comes from the ancient Greek optikē, meaning 'appearance, look'.

paragraphs.heading: How does seeing work
paragraphs.text: Greek thinkers split into two camps over how vision works. In the intromission theory, objects shed copies of themselves, called eidola, which the eye catches. In the emission theory, first set out by Plato, the eyes send out rays. Euclid wrote a book called Optics that tied vision to geometry and so created geometrical optics, yet he doubted that a beam from the eye could light up the stars instantly every time someone blinked. Ptolemy, in his own Optics, summed up much of Euclid and described a way to measure the angle of refraction.

paragraphs.heading: Advances in the Muslim world
paragraphs.text: In the Middle Ages, writers in the Muslim world revived Greek ideas about optics and pushed them further. In 984 the Persian mathematician Ibn Sahl correctly described a law of refraction equal to Snell's law and used it to work out the best shapes for lenses and curved mirrors. In the early 11th century, Alhazen wrote the Book of Optics, grounding his account of light and vision in observation and experiment. He rejected the idea of rays leaving the eye and argued that light bounces in straight lines in every direction from each point of an object and then enters the eye. Translated into Latin around 1200, his work became a standard optics text in Europe for the next 400 years.

paragraphs.heading: Light comes from objects
paragraphs.text: Roger Bacon, the best-known follower of the 13th-century English bishop Robert Grosseteste, drew on many freshly translated works, Alhazen's among them. Using parts of glass spheres as magnifying glasses, he showed that light reflects off objects rather than being given off by them.
